analysis.title: 'Elice' Crash Vs 'Compromise' Dash: Crude & CoreWeave Battle In 'Squeezy' Tape
key_insights: Korean data-center firm Elice fell 32% on its IPO debut after a 400x oversubscribed offering, setting an 'Anything but AI' tone overnight. The day then reversed on Iran deal 'compromise' headlines that sent crude lower and lifted stocks, bonds, gold and bitcoin.
A denial that Iran-US deal reports were accurate sent oil back to roughly unchanged. Yields rose back up, the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) ended red, and the dollar and gold both fell on the day.
Data-center CDS spreads hit a new record wide. Hyperscaler CDS was stable at record wides. CoreWeave (CRWV) bonds sold off at the open, recovered with equities, and ended basically unchanged.

Bloomberg's Michael Ball cites signs that markets question whether every AI project deserves increasingly expensive capital: Elice's 32% IPO drop, Firmus shelving its offering, valuation pushback at Nscale, and CoreWeave bond yields near 15%.

Brent hit a 5-month high above $110 overnight after Iranian state media reported a supertanker struck a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz. Goldman's Daan Struyven said futures price a significant probability of escalation or a longer Middle East conflict.
WTI (Dec) rallied above $101 before the 'compromise' headlines, then the denial pulled it back to unchanged. Dated Brent was modestly higher for a second day. US and EU diesel ended around unchanged.

European natural gas fell sharply after touching EUR 90 for the first time in almost four years. Rabobank's Florence Schmit sees potential to go above that level again within a week. EU gas storage is about 75% full, the lowest for the season since 2009, and Germany is just over 61%.

Bonds decoupled from crude: the short end underperformed the long end despite weak housing data. ING's Padhraic Garvey sees a bond-bullish tint across the US data. RBC's Izaac Brook says the AI risk-off trade from last week is driving rates, with lower oil also helping.
France's CDS hit a new cycle high, the worst among the PFIIGS. Rate-hike odds dipped modestly, with a December move still fully priced and the Fed in its blackout period.

Stocks rallied hard on the Iran headline, led by small caps, with a big ramp in 'Most Shorted' stocks. None of the majors made higher highs than the initial spike, and NDX closed red. SPX rose back above its 50-day moving average early, then faded back to it and found support.

Goldman traders saw activity around 4 out of 10 with franchise flows skewed 4% better to buy. Long-only accounts were 2.4% better to buy (demand in macro products and consumer staples, supply in communication services and utilities). Hedge funds were 2.5% better for sale (supply in energy, utilities, real estate).

The S&P 493 outperformed the Mag7. AI stocks underperformed after a large round trip in the first couple of hours. NeoClouds fell over 4% early, rallied to almost +3%, and ended unchanged. Momentum continued to fade, and memory stocks reverted lower after a one-day bounce. SPX ex-AI is catching up to SPX YTD performance.

Option positioning shows the AI trade splitting in two (Bloomberg's Ball, citing SpotGamma and MenthorQ): investors pay up for downside in higher-beta infrastructure names while keeping selective upside in quality semiconductors. Single-stock and semi-index skew has moved from call-heavy toward puts, and implied volatility has risen. Susquehanna flags call buying in DRAM and SOXX, mostly through spreads that cap gains to offset high implied volatility.
TSMC and ASML earnings showed strong long-term demand. Ball reads the correction as a positioning unwind and says AI capex is becoming more selective, not collapsing.
VIX options expire tomorrow. Many long VIX puts printed on Friday and could come into play on the last trading day.

Bitcoin rose above $83k, toward the upper end of the last two weeks' range, and traded as the same trade as CRWV. The dollar fell back to three-week lows and gold lost ground despite the weaker dollar.

Ball argues cheaper, more distributed compute (the Apple-Meta push to run open-weight models locally) collides with costlier capital. Credit investors want wider spreads, lower advance rates, more sponsor equity and stronger guarantees. This raises the hurdle rate for marginal projects and makes delays or cancellations more likely before payments are missed.

Credit markets are moving with token costs, while equities lean on the Jevons Paradox. The author says deflation is running ahead of adoption. Ball expects greater dispersion and rotation between winners and losers, with bouts of higher index volatility.

tension_points.bull_case: Cheaper compute broadens AI adoption and productivity. TSMC and ASML show strong long-term demand, and capex is becoming selective rather than collapsing. Equities lean on the Jevons Paradox.
tension_points.bear_case: Capital is costlier: wider credit spreads, lower advance rates and more sponsor equity demanded. Data-center CDS is at record wides, and neocloud IPOs and offerings are struggling. Deflation in compute is running ahead of adoption.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further data-center CDS widening or more IPO and offering withdrawals would confirm the bear case. A CoreWeave bond yield falling well below 15% would undercut it.

theme_stances.key_argument: The AI trade is now in a stock-picker phase where cheaper compute collides with more expensive capital, weakening the most capital-intensive parts of the buildout.
theme_stances.evidence: cheaper and more distributed compute collides with more expensive capital

theme_stances.key_argument: Reports of an Iran deal are treated as spurious headlines that drove a short squeeze before a denial reversed them.
